intro.t: Forty years of wandering, and why.
b: Israel arrives at the edge of the promised land within two years and refuses to enter. The rest of the book is the cost of that refusal. It is a sustained study in unbelief among people who had personally watched the sea part.
The generation that leaves Egypt is not the generation that enters. That is the warning Hebrews 3–4 draws from it.

6.t: Voluntary, temporary, and marked by abstaining from wine and leaving the hair uncut. Samson and Samuel were both under it from birth.
The Aaronic blessing, still used weekly in churches. The oldest known fragment of biblical text is a silver amulet carrying it.

13.t: Ten spies report giants, two report God. The nation believes the ten and spends forty years in consequence.
In our own eyes, and we looked the same to them. The report is accurate about the giants and wrong about God.

11.t: Moses asks God whether he conceived this people. The Spirit is put on seventy elders, and Moses wishes all the LORD's people were prophets.

12.t: They challenge Moses over his Cushite wife and over his standing. Moses, described as the most humble man on earth, prays for Miriam's healing.

14.t: They say it would be better to die in Egypt, and God takes them at their word. Caleb and Joshua alone of that generation enter.

16.t: A challenge to Moses' and Aaron's authority that ends in the ground opening. Jude 11 uses it as a warning. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

20.t: Moses is told to speak to it and hits it twice. The cost is that he does not enter the land — which reads as severe until you notice what he claimed in verse 10.

22.t: A pagan seer hired to curse Israel, and a donkey with better spiritual sight than its owner. 2 Peter and Jude both use him as a picture of teaching for money.

1.t: A fighting force counted at Sinai. The book's English name comes from this; the Hebrew name is 'In the wilderness', which fits it better.

3.h: The Levites instead of the firstborn
3.t: Taken in place of every firstborn son God claimed at the Passover. Substitution built into the structure of Israel's worship.

9.t: They moved when it lifted and stayed when it settled, however long that was. Guidance as obedience to something you do not control.

10.t: Moses asks his brother-in-law to come with them, despite the cloud. Divine guidance and local knowledge are not treated as rivals.

15.t: A visible reminder on the edge of the garment so they would remember the commands. The woman with the bleeding touched the edge of Jesus' cloak.

21.t: Looking at the image of the thing killing them brings life. Jesus applies it to himself in John 3:14.

23.h: God is not a man, that he should lie
23.t: Spoken by Balaam, of all people, and one of the clearest statements of God's constancy in Scripture.

27.t: Five women petition for an inheritance and the law is changed in their favour. Moses takes the case to God rather than dismissing it.

32.h: The two and a half tribes
32.t: They want land east of the Jordan and are made to fight for their brothers first. Settling early is permitted; leaving others to fight is not.

35.t: Six towns where someone who killed accidentally could flee the avenger. Ancient law distinguishing manslaughter from murder.

2.t: Every tribe in position, with God's dwelling at the centre. The layout itself is theology.

4.t: The Kohathites carry the sacred objects but may not look at them. The Uzzah incident in 2 Samuel 6 turns on exactly this.

5.h: The test for a suspected wife
5.t: An ordeal ritual that troubles modern readers. In its setting it removed the matter from the husband's hands and placed it before God, which was a protection as well as a test. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

7.t: The longest chapter in the Pentateuch, repeating the same gift twelve times. Every tribe's gift is recorded in full, as if each mattered individually.

8.t: Given to Aaron as a gift from the people. Their service begins at twenty-five and ends at fifty.

17.t: It buds, blossoms and produces almonds overnight — God settling a dispute about leadership with something only he could do.

18.t: The Levites receive no land. God himself is their inheritance, and the tithe supports them.

19.t: A cleansing ritual for contact with death. Hebrews 9 contrasts its outward cleansing with Christ's cleansing of the conscience.

24.t: Balaam, hired to curse, prophesies a king. Early Jewish and Christian readers alike took it as messianic.

25.t: Where Balaam's curses failed, his advice succeeded: seduction into idolatry. Revelation 2 names Balaam's teaching as the cause.

26.t: A new generation counted. Not one of the first census remained except Caleb and Joshua.

28.t: Every morning and every evening, without exception. Worship built into the rhythm of every day.

29.t: Trumpets, Atonement and Tabernacles, with their offerings. The number of bulls at Tabernacles decreases daily from thirteen to seven.

30.t: A woman's vow could be annulled by her father or husband on the day he heard it. The law assumes household responsibility; the principle for everyone is to keep your word.

31.t: One of the most difficult chapters in Scripture, and it should not be read quickly or explained away. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

33.t: A list of forty-two stages from Egypt to the Jordan. The journey is remembered stop by stop.

34.t: The land described precisely. The promise to Abraham becomes a map.

36.t: The book ends by protecting the inheritance of five women. Numbers closes on a small detail of justice.
